2. Look at what you got

a. What range of dates does the file cover?
2021-09-01 to 2026-09-01


b. Interval
What is the interval — hourly, daily, weekly, monthly? Now change the date window and download again csv. Did the interval change?
The five-year dataset uses monthly observations. After changing the window to “Last 24 hours,” the interval changed to 16 minutes because Google Trends automatically adjusts its temporal resolution to the selected time window.


c. What are the units? What does a value of 100 mean, and 0?
These are a normalized search-interest index from 0–100, based on the proportion of searches for the term relative to all searches in the selected place and time period.

100 = the point of peak relative search interest within the selected dataset.
50 = relative search interest was half the peak level.
0 = insufficient search volume to report a value; it does not necessarily mean zero searches occurred.



d. Now remove one search term and download again.
Did the numbers for the remaining terms stay the same?
Dropped Trump from the Past 5 years search. The values for Kamala Harris and Election stayed exactly the same across all 61 monthly observations. Removing Trump did not alter the scale in this comparison because Election still supplied the peak value of 100, while Trump had a maximum value of 40. csv

3. Collect it from R

a. gtrends package
Use the gtrendsR package and the gtrendsR01.R program. The first call in that script is the same query you just ran by hand:

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

# Store successful Google Trends downloads here.
cache_dir <- "_gtrends_cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Download each query only once. If Google temporarily blocks the request,
# retry with exponential backoff until a successful result is returned.
# Once saved as an RDS file, future renders read the local file and never
# contact Google Trends for that query again.
cached_gtrends <- function(cache_name, ..., initial_wait = 60, max_wait = 600) {
  cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, cache_name)

  if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
    return(readRDS(cache_file))
  }

  attempt <- 1L

  repeat {
    result <- tryCatch(
      gtrends(...),
      error = function(e) {
        message(
          "Google Trends request failed on attempt ", attempt,
          ": ", conditionMessage(e)
        )
        NULL
      }
    )

    if (!is.null(result)) {
      saveRDS(result, cache_file)
      message("Google Trends data saved to: ", cache_file)
      return(result)
    }

    wait <- min(initial_wait * 2^(attempt - 1L), max_wait)
    wait <- wait + runif(1, 0, 15)
    message("Retrying in ", round(wait), " seconds...")
    Sys.sleep(wait)
    attempt <- attempt + 1L
  }
}

TrumpHarrisElection <- cached_gtrends(
  "trump_harris_election_us_5y.rds",
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

A note on terms The website instructions above say Kamala Harris. The script searches Harris.

a. Pull both and compare the series. Are they the same?

  c("Harris", "Kamala Harris"),

harris_numeric <- harris_compare$interest_over_time |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    hits_numeric = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(hits))),
    hits_numeric = dplyr::if_else(
      as.character(hits) == "<1",
      0.5,
      hits_numeric
    )
  )

harris_means <- harris_numeric |>
  dplyr::group_by(keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    observations = dplyr::n(),
    mean_interest = mean(hits_numeric),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

harris_by_date <- harris_numeric |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Harris") |>
  dplyr::select(date, harris = hits_numeric) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    harris_numeric |>
      dplyr::filter(keyword == "Kamala Harris") |>
      dplyr::select(date, kamala_harris = hits_numeric),
    by = "date"
  )

harris_gap <- harris_by_date |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    matched_dates = dplyr::n(),
    dates_harris_higher = sum(harris > kamala_harris),
    mean_gap = mean(harris - kamala_harris)
  )

harris_means

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  keyword       observations mean_interest
  <chr>                <int>         <dbl>
1 Harris                 262          9.19
2 Kamala Harris          262          2.02

harris_gap

  matched_dates dates_harris_higher mean_gap
1           262                 262 7.171756


The Harris and Kamala Harris series are not the same. Across 262 weekly observations, the mean Google Trends index was 9.19 for Harris and 2.02 for Kamala Harris, an average gap of 7.17 points. Harris had the higher value on all 262 dates. These normalized values show relative interest within this joint comparison; they are not raw search counts.


b. Harris
Harris is also a county, a supermarket chain, and several thousand other people. What does that gap tell you about the difference between a search term and the concept you meant to measure?
This gap shows that a search term is not necessarily identical to the concept being measured. Harris is an ambiguous term that can capture searches concerning Kamala Harris as well as unrelated people, places, and organizations. The results do not reveal how much of the broader Harris series actually concerns Kamala Harris. Therefore, using Harris to measure interest in Kamala Harris introduces measurement error, while the more specific Kamala Harris query better represents the intended concept.

title: Assignment 02
text:
4. Compare the two methods

a. Line the two series up. Are the numbers identical? If not, by how much, and in which direction?
The website query used Kamala Harris, while the R script used Harris. To avoid treating those different search terms as equivalent, this comparison uses the two terms shared by both pulls: Trump and Election. The website data are monthly, whereas the R data are weekly, so the R observations are averaged by month and rescaled to a 0–100 index. The incomplete first and last months are excluded, leaving 59 complete months for each term.

website_common <- read_csv(
  "time_series_US_20210912-0854_20260912-0854.csv",
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::select(date = Time, Trump, Election) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = -date,
    names_to = "keyword",
    values_to = "website_hits"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    date >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
    date <= as.Date("2026-08-01")
  )

r_monthly <- the_df |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword %in% c("Trump", "election")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    keyword = dplyr::recode(keyword, election = "Election"),
    r_hits = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(as.character(hits))),
    r_hits = dplyr::if_else(as.character(hits) == "<1", 0.5, r_hits),
    date = as.Date(date),
    month = as.Date(format(date, "%Y-%m-01"))
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(month, keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    r_monthly_mean = mean(r_hits),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    month >= as.Date("2021-10-01"),
    month <= as.Date("2026-08-01")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    r_monthly_index = 100 * r_monthly_mean / max(r_monthly_mean)
  )

method_comparison <- website_common |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    r_monthly,
    by = c("date" = "month", "keyword")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    difference = r_monthly_index - website_hits,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

method_comparison_by_term <- method_comparison |>
  dplyr::group_by(keyword) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    months = dplyr::n(),
    mean_website = mean(website_hits),
    mean_r = mean(r_monthly_index),
    mean_difference = mean(difference),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference),
    correlation = cor(website_hits, r_monthly_index),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

method_comparison_overall <- method_comparison |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    observations_compared = dplyr::n(),
    observations_different = sum(abs(difference) > 1e-9),
    mean_difference = mean(difference),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference)
  )

election_comparison <- method_comparison_by_term |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Election")

trump_comparison <- method_comparison_by_term |>
  dplyr::filter(keyword == "Trump")

method_comparison_by_term

2 Trump        59        10.7   10.3           -0.401                    0.719

method_comparison |>
  dplyr::select(date, keyword, Website = website_hits, R = r_monthly_index) |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(Website, R),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "interest"
  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
    ggplot2::aes(x = date, y = interest, color = method)
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~keyword, ncol = 1) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    x = "Date",
    y = "Relative search interest",
    color = "Source"
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()




Monthly Google Trends indices from the website and R for the two shared search terms, October 2021–August 2026.




The numbers are not identical: 117 of 118 matched term-month observations differed. Across both terms, the mean absolute difference was 0.81 points and the maximum absolute difference was 4.61 points. On average, the R index for Election was 0.52 points higher than the website index, while the R index for Trump was 0.4 points lower. Despite the small numerical differences, the series have very similar shapes: their correlations are 0.997 for Election and 0.994 for Trump. This remains an approximate comparison because the original queries used different Harris terms and Google Trends relies on sampled, normalized data.


b. What are the differences between the two methods? Consider at least:

i. Reproducibility — could someone else regenerate your file exactly?
Neither method guarantees that another person can reproduce the exact values by making a new request, because Google Trends draws from sampled data and a moving “last five years” window. The R method makes the procedure more reproducible because the code records the query and analysis steps. Exact numerical reproduction depends on retaining and sharing the cached raw data used for the analysis.


ii. Provenance — which method records the query parameters for you?
The R method provides stronger provenance because the function call explicitly records the search terms, geography, time window, category, and search type. The website download requires those selections and the pull time to be documented manually in a datasheet; the CSV alone does not preserve the complete collection procedure.


iii. Scale — what happens when you need fifty terms instead of three?
Collecting fifty terms manually would require many repeated website searches and downloads, increasing both labor and the risk of inconsistent settings. R can automate the repeated calls, file naming, validation, and caching. However, the terms must still be divided into batches because the service limits comparisons, and the batches need a shared anchor term if their separately normalized indices are to be placed on a common scale.


iv. Fragility — what breaks, and how would you know?
The website method is vulnerable to interface changes, inconsistent manual selections, and misplaced downloads. The R method depends on gtrendsR and an unofficial endpoint, so changes to the service can break requests or parsing; rate limiting can also return errors such as HTTP 429. Failures should be detected by checking request errors, expected columns, date ranges, row counts, missing values, and the 0–100 range before analysis. Caching the first successful pull prevents later endpoint failures from changing an already completed analysis.



c. Run section 7 of the script: the same call twice, a few minutes apart.
Do you get the same numbers?

# These use two different cache files intentionally so the assignment captures
# two Google Trends samples collected three minutes apart. Each sample is
# downloaded only once.
first_cache_name <- "repeat_trump_harris_election_spaced_1.rds"
second_cache_name <- "repeat_trump_harris_election_spaced_2.rds"

repeat_pull_1 <- cached_gtrends(
  first_cache_name,
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

# Wait only when the second sample has not yet been cached. Later renders reuse
# both files without waiting or contacting Google Trends again.
second_cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, second_cache_name)

if (!file.exists(second_cache_file)) {
  message("Waiting three minutes before the second pull...")
  Sys.sleep(180)
}

repeat_pull_2 <- cached_gtrends(
  second_cache_name,
  c("Trump", "Harris", "election"),
  onlyInterest = TRUE,
  geo = "US",
  gprop = "web",
  time = "today+5-y",
  category = 0
)

repeat_pull_times <- data.frame(
  pull = c("Pull 1", "Pull 2"),
  cached_at = file.info(
    file.path(
      cache_dir,
      c(first_cache_name, second_cache_name)
    )
  )$mtime
)

repeat_pull_times

    pull           cached_at
1 Pull 1 2026-09-15 09:12:36
2 Pull 2 2026-09-15 09:15:37

pull_1 <- repeat_pull_1$interest_over_time
pull_2 <- repeat_pull_2$interest_over_time

# Convert Google Trends scores to numbers.
# "<1" is represented by its midpoint, 0.5.
hits_to_numeric <- function(x) {
  x <- as.character(x)
  result <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  result[x == "<1"] <- 0.5
  result
}

pull_comparison <- pull_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    date,
    keyword,
    hits_1_raw = hits,
    hits_1 = hits_to_numeric(hits)
  ) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(
    pull_2 |>
      dplyr::transmute(
        date,
        keyword,
        hits_2_raw = hits,
        hits_2 = hits_to_numeric(hits)
      ),
    by = c("date", "keyword")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    difference = hits_2 - hits_1,
    absolute_difference = abs(difference)
  )

pull_summary <- pull_comparison |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    exactly_identical = all(hits_1_raw == hits_2_raw),
    observations_compared = dplyr::n(),
    observations_different = sum(hits_1_raw != hits_2_raw),
    mean_absolute_difference = mean(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE),
    maximum_absolute_difference = max(absolute_difference, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

pull_summary

  exactly_identical observations_compared observations_different
1             FALSE                   786                     15
  mean_absolute_difference maximum_absolute_difference
1                0.0178117                           1


The two pulls did not return exactly the same values. Of the 786 matched observations, 15 differed. The mean absolute difference was 0.02 points, and the maximum absolute difference was 1 point.
The first pull was cached at 2026-09-15 09:12:36 CDT, and the second was cached at 2026-09-15 09:15:37 CDT.
What does your answer imply about every finding you might report from this source?
Because Google Trends uses sampled and normalized search data, its values should be interpreted as estimates rather than exact counts. Repeated pulls may produce slightly different values, although the broad pattern may remain stable. Each successful pull should therefore be cached, documented, and interpreted without overemphasizing small numerical differences.

3. Weekly challenge — causal structure

What is causal inference? Be able to say it in two sentences.

Causal inference is the process of determining whether a change in one factor causes a change in another. Data, along with statistical methods, are used to estimate what would have happened under a counterfactual if something had been different.

Draw a causal diagram of something from existing research or your own project — a DAG: nodes are variables, arrows are causal claims.

Mark at least one confounder — a common cause of two variables — and a collider if you have one.
Draw it with ggdag in R, or at https://www.dagitty.net.










Figure 1: Causal diagram of period and trip trajectory.





Figure 1 shows the assumed causal structure. Period, the exposure, can affect trajectory characteristics along two routes. The green paths run through destination POI type and represent composition (H1). The blue path is the effect of period within destination type and represents the temporal account (H2). H3 holds if both routes carry weight. Individual, origin location, and calendar (hour, day type, season) are confounders, because each is a common cause of period and trajectory. Destination POI type is also a collider, because period and origin both point into it. Holding destination type constant therefore opens a path from period through origin to trajectory, so the model that holds destination type constant must also adjust for origin. Trip purpose is unobserved and is assumed to reach trajectory only through destination type. Stops coded by hand test that assumption by period.

text:
3. Get a YouTube Data API key

Create a Google account if you do not have one — your own name as the account ID, no birthday or year in it.
Open the Google Cloud Console — https://console.cloud.google.com — and create a project; it is just a container for the key.
APIs & Services → Library → YouTube Data API v3 → Enable. Nothing works until the API is enabled on that project.
APIs & Services → Credentials → Create credentials → API key. Copy it, then Restrict key to the YouTube Data API.
Google’s Create access credentials — https://developers.google.com/workspace/guides/create-credentials

You probably do not need OAuth. An API key covers everything this course does — reading public data: search, videos, channels, playlists, comments. An OAuth 2.0 client ID and secret is needed only to write, or to read a signed-in user’s private data.
Quota. A new project gets 100 search.list calls plus 10,000 units/day across other endpoints; most reads cost 1 unit — so search is the scarce resource. Collect IDs once, cache them, page through cheaper endpoints. And treat the key like the Census key: never in a .qmd, never committed.

Prepare answers to: (i) what is a Bayesian network? (ii) compare causation with correlation.

Bayesian Network

A Bayesian network is a probabilistic model that represents relationships among variables using a directed acyclic graph (DAG).

Causation / Correlation

Correlation means that two variables are statistically linked. When one changes, the other tends to change in some way. Correlation does not establish why the association exists.


Causation means that changing one thing produces a change in another thing.


For instance ice-cream sales and heat-related illnesses may be positively correlated, but buying ice cream does not necessarily cause heat stroke.

Getting familiar with data import in R.

What are the most commonly used packages for importing data in R?


readr — delimited text files such as CSV
readxl — Excel files
haven — SPSS, Stata, and SAS files
jsonlite — JSON
xml2 — XML
arrow — Parquet, Feather, and Arrow IPC

For geospatial data, some of the common packages are:

sf — vector geospatial data such as Shapefile, GeoPackage, and GeoJSON
terra — raster geospatial data such as GeoTIFF and other GDAL-supported formats
stars — multidimensional raster and spatiotemporal data
lidR — LiDAR point-cloud data such as LAS and LAZ
rnaturalearth — Natural Earth country, boundary, coastline, and physical geography
gdalcubes — access and process large collections of Earth observation imagery
osmdata — OpenStreetMap data through the Overpass API
tigris — U.S. Census TIGER/Line geographic data


Conventional formats — CSV, SPSS, Stata, XML, JSON. Be able to name what reads each one.





Format
Common R package/function




CSV
readr::read_csv()


SPSS
haven::read_sav()


Stata
haven::read_dta()


XML
xml2::read_xml()


JSON
jsonlite::fromJSON()




New formats — Feather, Parquet, Arrow IPC, ORC, HDF5, Zarr, Avro. What problem does each one solve that CSV does not?








Format
Main advantage over CSV




Feather
Fast, typed, columnar exchange between data-analysis systems


Parquet
Compressed columnar storage optimized for large analytical datasets


Arrow IPC
Fast in-memory or interprocess exchange without repeated serialization


ORC
Compressed columnar storage designed for large-scale analytical workloads


HDF5
Efficient storage of large, complex, multidimensional scientific data


Zarr
Chunked, compressed multidimensional arrays suited to cloud/object storage


Avro
Schema-based row-oriented serialization useful for data exchange and streaming



New data formats exist because CSV is simple and portable but does not preserve data types, efficiently compress large datasets, support fast columnar access, or handle complex and multidimensional data well. This is especially problematic with geospatial data.
Bring the activated Census API key and the one-sentence explanation of why the new formats exist; class begins by pulling Census data live.

a. Geography

Counties in the state of Texas


b. Variables
Variables: at least two. For example B19013_001 (median household income) and B17001_002 (people below poverty).

title: Assignment 3
text:
3. Download, with geometry

a. get_acs
Use get_acs() with your geography and variables, geometry = TRUE.


b. Estimate and Margin of Error
Keep the estimate and the margin of error. Every ACS number is an estimate from a sample; the MOE is not decoration.

acs_file <- paste0("acs_", state_abbr, "_", year_acs, ".csv")

if (file.exists(acs_file)) {

  acs_data <- read_csv(
    acs_file,
    col_types = cols(
      GEOID = col_character(),
      .default = col_guess()
    )
  )

  county_geom <- counties(
    state = state_abbr,
    year = year_acs,
    cb = TRUE,
    class = "sf"
  ) |>
    select(GEOID, geometry)

  acs_wide <- county_geom |>
    left_join(acs_data, by = "GEOID")

} else {

  acs_wide <- get_acs(
    geography = geo_level,
    variables = my_vars,
    state = state_abbr,
    year = year_acs,
    survey = survey,
    geometry = TRUE,
    output = "wide"
  )

  write_csv(
    st_drop_geometry(acs_wide),
    acs_file
  )
}


# 5) Derive bachelor's degree or higher rate and carry the MOE through
acs_wide <- acs_wide |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(
    bachelors_plus = sum(
      c(bachelorsE, mastersE, professionalE, doctorateE)
    ),
    bachelors_plus_moe = moe_sum(
      c(bachelorsM, mastersM, professionalM, doctorateM),
      c(bachelorsE, mastersE, professionalE, doctorateE)
    ),
    bachelors_plus_rate = bachelors_plus / edu_totalE,
    bachelors_plus_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      bachelors_plus,
      edu_totalE,
      bachelors_plus_moe,
      edu_totalM
    )

  ungroup()

c. Uncertainty check
Uncertainty check — name one pair of areas in your table whose confidence intervals overlap. What does that do to the ranking you just published?

uncertainty_check <- edu_table |>
  mutate(
    lower = `Bachelor's degree or higher (%)` - `MOE (%)`,
    upper = `Bachelor's degree or higher (%)` + `MOE (%)`
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(`Bachelor's degree or higher (%)`)) |>
  mutate(
    next_county = lead(County),
    next_lower = lead(lower),
    next_upper = lead(upper),
    overlap = lower <= next_upper & upper >= next_lower
  ) |>
  filter(overlap) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

uncertainty_check

# A tibble: 1 × 10
  Group  County         Bachelor's degree or…¹ `MOE (%)` lower upper next_county
  <chr>  <chr>                           <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <chr>      
1 Top 10 Travis County…                   56.6       0.7  55.9  57.3 Collin Cou…
# ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​`Bachelor's degree or higher (%)`
# ℹ 3 more variables: next_lower <dbl>, next_upper <dbl>, overlap <lgl>


Travis County has an estimated bachelor’s-degree-or-higher rate of 56.6%, with a margin of error of ±0.7 percentage points. Its confidence interval therefore extends from approximately 55.9% to 57.3%. This interval overlaps with the confidence interval for Collin County. Although Travis County ranks above Collin County based on the point estimates, the overlapping intervals indicate that this ordering should not be treated as definitive.
Loving County provides an even stronger example of uncertainty in the rankings. Its estimated bachelor’s-degree-or-higher rate is 0.0%, but the margin of error is ±48.4 percentage points. This very large uncertainty means that its position at the bottom of the table should not be interpreted as a precise ranking. The result illustrates how small-population counties can have highly uncertain ACS estimates.


d. Methods note
Methods note (≤ 200 words) — your choices of geography and variables, and what the MOEs do to your interpretation.

This analysis uses 2024 ACS 5-year estimates for all counties in Texas. County geography was selected because it provides a useful balance between statewide coverage and local variation. Using counties makes it possible to compare patterns across Texas without producing a map that is too detailed or difficult to read.
The two variables used are median age and educational attainment. Median age comes from B01002_001. Educational attainment is measured as the percentage of the population age 25 and older with a bachelor’s degree or higher. This measure was calculated by combining the bachelor’s, master’s, professional, and doctoral degree categories from ACS table B15003 and dividing that total by the population age 25 and older.
Margins of error were retained because ACS values are estimates based on a sample rather than a complete count. The margins of error for the education measure were propagated through both the combined degree categories and the final percentage calculation. This affects interpretation because counties with similar estimates may have overlapping confidence intervals. When intervals overlap, the apparent difference between two counties may not be meaningful, so the exact ranking should be treated cautiously rather than as a definitive ordering.


e. Publish
Publish as assign03.qmd under Assignments on your website.

title: Assignment 3
text:
Notes

Prefer rates to counts where a denominator exists, and propagate the MOE with moe_prop(), moe_ratio() or moe_sum() rather than dropping it.
Mapping tracts or block groups for a whole state is slow and unreadable — filter to one county or metro area first.

Two different caches. options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE) caches map geometry and is still correct. The cache argument of load_variables() is not: current tidycensus reports it “deprecated and ignored — variable metadata is now loaded from the Census API without writing to a local cache.” Drop it.

section: 5. Discuss — a comment section as data
text:
5. Discuss — a comment section as data

Who writes YouTube comments, and who reads them? Who never appears?
What edits them — channel moderation, held-for-review filters, YouTube’s ranking (order = "relevance"), deletions?
What selects the comments you can collect: the search ranking, the video, the channel, your max_results, the day you ran it?
The API terms allow you to keep this data 30 days. What does that mean for reproducibility — and for your website?


a. Who writes, who reads, who never appears
A small, self-selected minority writes comments, and a few accounts write most of them. Commenters lean toward people with strong views, and they include spam accounts, bots, coordinated campaigns, and the channel owner. Many more people read than write. Most viewers never comment, so the comment section measures the engaged tail, not the audience.
Several groups never appear:

Viewers who watch silently.
People who don’t use YouTube at all. They skew older and toward places with poor broadband, which matters for a siting question.
Anyone whose comment was removed or held.
Every viewer of a video with comments disabled. Made-for-Kids videos have comments turned off automatically.

For your project, the people who live next to a proposed facility may be far less visible than national commentators. Because comments carry no location, you can’t tell the two apart.


b. What edits them
Comments pass through several filters before you see them:

The commenter: People edit their own comments, which is why updated_at exists.
The creator: Creators can delete comments, hide users, block words, and hold comments for review. Held comments aren’t public, so the API never returns them.
YouTube: Automated spam filters hold comments, and policy enforcement removes them.
Ranking: The call above uses the API default, order = "time", so truncation favors recent comment threads. If order = "relevance" is requested, truncation favors comments YouTube ranks as relevant.
Partial replies: commentThreads.list returns top-level threads and may include only some replies. A fuller collection would follow up with comments.list for replies.
Timing: Deletion can happen after you collect a comment. A stored corpus can therefore contain comments that are no longer public, which matters for (d).



c. What selects what you can collect
Each layer narrows the sample:

Search: search.list returns a relevance-ranked sample, not a complete list. It is shaped by the query, regionCode, relevanceLanguage, pagination, and the day of collection.
The video and channel: Their audience, moderation norms, and whether comments are enabled all shape what is available.
max_results and paging: With the default time ordering, stopping after 100 selects recent top-level threads, not a random 100. With relevance ordering, it selects the threads YouTube ranks most highly.
The day you ran it: Comments keep arriving, and some get edited or deleted. nrow(cmts) can differ from get_video_stats() because the former counts retrieved top-level threads and the latter reports a broader total that includes replies.
Quota: Quota and endpoint-specific call limits constrain how much can be collected.

For this exercise, the corpus is a sample of publicly visible top-level comments, at the time of collection, on the latest upload from one fixed channel. In a search-based project, YouTube’s ranking of videos adds another selection layer. Neither corpus is a sample of public opinion; its frame is defined by the query or channel, video-selection rule, API filters, collection time, and result limit.


d. The 30-day rule: reproducibility and your website
Section III.E.4 of the policy is specific:

Data collected with only an API key is “Non-Authorized Data.”
You may store limited amounts of it temporarily, for no more than 30 days. After that you must delete it or refresh it.
The same limit applies to statistics like view counts and subscriber counts.
Stored data must reasonably match what YouTube currently shows.

Three consequences:

You can’t publish a frozen comment corpus for others to rerun. Reproducibility moves from sharing data to sharing code, queries, collection dates, and a clear description of the sampling process.
Re-collection won’t match exactly. Re-pulling the same IDs later can return a different set because comments are added, deleted, or edited.
The research design is affected. A plan for frozen, hashed weekly snapshots or a sealed estimation sample conflicts with the 30-day refresh-or-delete rule for Non-Authorized Data. Section III.E.4.h also restricts derived metrics from API data. The project should confirm what is permitted under the applicable terms or a research authorization before retaining long-term snapshots or publishing derived scores.

For the website:

Keep Parquet files and raw comment text out of the public repository with .gitignore.
Check rendered output carefully: Quarto’s _freeze folder and rendered HTML can preserve printed comment text or API statistics.
Publish the collection code, queries, dates, and sampling description. Publish aggregate or derived results only after confirming that the applicable YouTube terms or research authorization permit them.

Sources:
(YouTube API Services – Developer Policies (§III.E.4, §III.E.6; last updated 2026-10-15))

text:
3. Download the documents

Using Part B of govtdata01.R, download the ten most recent hearings of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations.


library(httr2)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(tibble)
library(readr)

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Configuration
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

key <- Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")

if (!nzchar(key)) {
  stop("GOVINFO_API_KEY is missing.")
}

n_target <- 10
max_candidates <- 100
page_size <- 25

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Base API request
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

govinfo <- function(path) {
  request(paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/", path)) |>
    req_url_query(api_key = key) |>
    req_retry(max_tries = 3)
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

search_page <- function(offset = "*") {

  govinfo("search") |>
    req_body_json(list(
      query = paste(
        "collection:CHRG",
        "AND chamber:senate",
        'AND committee:("foreign relations")'
      ),
      pageSize = page_size,
      offsetMark = offset,
      sorts = list(
        list(
          field = "publishdate",
          sortOrder = "DESC"
        )
      )
    )) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json()
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Retrieve package metadata
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

get_summary <- function(id) {

  tryCatch({

    govinfo(paste0("packages/", id, "/summary")) |>
      req_perform() |>
      resp_body_json()

  }, error = function(e) {

    warning(
      "Could not retrieve package ", id,
      ": ", conditionMessage(e)
    )

    NULL
  })
}

# -------------------------------------------------------------------
# Search for ten qualifying hearings
# -------------------------------------------------------------------

selected_hearings <- list()
seen <- character()
offset <- "*"

while (
  length(selected_hearings) < n_target &&
  length(seen) < max_candidates
) {

  page <- search_page(offset)

  results <- page$results

  if (is.null(results) || length(results) == 0) {
    break
  }

  # Process search results
  for (result in results) {

    if (
      length(selected_hearings) >= n_target ||
      length(seen) >= max_candidates
    ) {
      break
    }

    id <- result$packageId

    if (
      is.null(id) ||
      !nzchar(id) ||
      id %in% seen
    ) {
      next
    }

    seen <- c(seen, id)

    # Senate hearing package IDs contain "shrg"
    if (!grepl("^CHRG-[0-9]+shrg", id, ignore.case = TRUE)) {
      next
    }

    # Retrieve metadata
    summary <- get_summary(id)

    Sys.sleep(0.5)

    if (is.null(summary)) {
      next
    }

    # Retain qualifying hearing
    selected_hearings[[id]] <- summary

    # Progress reporting
    cat(
      "Examined:", length(seen),
      "| Found:", length(selected_hearings),
      "of", n_target, "\n"
    )

    if (length(selected_hearings) >= n_target) {
      break
    }
  }

  # Stop if complete or capped
  if (
    length(selected_hearings) >= n_target ||
    length(seen) >= max_candidates
  ) {
    break
  }

  # Move to next page
  next_offset <- page$offsetMark

  if (
    is.null(next_offset) ||
    identical(next_offset, offset)
  ) {
    break
  }

  offset <- next_offset
}

# Initialize with required columns to prevent empty-table errors
hearing_tbl <- tibble(
  packageId = character(),
  title = character(),
  dateIssued = character(),

# Extract metadata
if (length(selected_hearings) > 0) {

  hearing_tbl <- map_dfr(selected_hearings, \(s) {

    download <- s$download

    if (is.null(download)) {
      download <- list()
    }

    # Hearing summaries often list only premisLink, zipLink and modsLink
    # (see section 2c), so fall back to the package content endpoints,

    pkg_url <- paste0("https://api.govinfo.gov/packages/", s$packageId)

      txtLink = download$txtLink %||% paste0(pkg_url, "/htm"),
      modsLink = download$modsLink %||% paste0(pkg_url, "/mods")
    )
  })
}

# Download function
download_pdf <- function(id, url) {

  dest <- file.path(pdf_dir, paste0(id, ".pdf"))

  started <- format(
    Sys.time(),
    "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %Z"
  )

  if (is.na(url) || !nzchar(url)) {

    result <- list(
      status = "no pdfLink",
      http = NA_integer_,
      error = NA_character_
    )

  } else {

    result <- tryCatch({

      response <- request(url) |>
        req_url_query(api_key = key) |>
        req_retry(max_tries = 3) |>
        req_perform(path = dest)

      list(
        status = "ok",
        http = resp_status(response),
        error = NA_character_
      )

    }, error = function(e) {

      list(
        status = "failed",
        http = NA_integer_,
        error = conditionMessage(e)
      )
    })
  }

  # Pause between downloads
  Sys.sleep(runif(1, 1, 3))

  tibble(
    packageId = id,
    pdf_url = url,
    file = dest,
    status = result$status,
    http_status = result$http,
    bytes = if (result$status == "ok") {
      file.size(dest)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    error = result$error,
    started = started
  )
}

4. Report
Write a short report on the difficulties you met.

How usable are the downloaded documents as data? What would it take to turn ten PDFs into a table or a corpus?

The PDFs are useful as sources but are not immediately useable for quantitative analysis. Converting them into a corpus would require extracting the text, removing formatting artifacts, and standardizing the documents. Scanned PDFs may also require OCR. Creating a structured table would require identifying fields such as hearing dates, committee names, speakers, and testimony, then validating the extracted information. This may currently be possible with some AI models.

How would you improve the process? Consider the other formats in download, and what the metadata gives you without opening a file.

The process could be improved by downloading text or XML files rather than PDFs if available. These formats are easier to parse and would reduce the need for text extraction or OCR. The API metadata already provides information such as titles, dates, IDs, and links, which allows the documents to be indexed and filtered. The main difficulties encountered were handling nested JSON responses, identifying the correct committee hearings, and managing pagination.
The largest problem was that the package summaries for these hearings listed only premisLink, zipLink and modsLink, with no pdfLink, so the first run downloaded nothing. Requesting each package’s PDF directly from /packages/{packageId}/pdf fixed it.

In two sentences: what did the API give you that the search page and last week’s scraping did not?

The API provided structured, machine-readable results. The API allowed direct access to document metadata and download links.

text:
4. Discuss —
Analytics of Text Data

a. How are text data generated?
For the hearings: who spoke, who edited, who printed, and what decided which ones you could collect?
Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
The hearings contain statements and testimony from senators, witnesses, and other participants. The published documents are products of a formal congressional process, including transcription, editing, and publication by the Government Publishing Office (GPO). Consequently, they are not necessarily verbatim records of everything said during a hearing.
Our collection is limited to hearings returned by the GovInfo API query, sorted by publication date. This introduces selection bias because the ten most recently published hearings are not necessarily the ten most recently conducted. The corpus also excludes hearings that have not yet been published or are unavailable through the API.


b. Topics —
what would a topic model find in ten SFRC hearings, and what would convince you it found something real?
Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
A topic model might identify recurring subjects such as national security, diplomatic relations, international conflicts, foreign assistance, or economic sanctions. However, these are plausible topics rather than findings from the ten hearings.
With only ten documents, topic modeling at the hearing level may produce unstable results. A larger number of observations could be obtained by dividing hearings into individual statements or testimony segments, although this would require careful segmentation.
I would validate the topics by examining the most influential words and representative passages, then comparing them against hearing titles, agendas, and substantive content.


c. Sentiment —
what would a dictionary make of diplomatic testimony? What does it miss?
Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
A dictionary-based sentiment model might classify testimony containing words such as “conflict,” “threat,” or “crisis” as negative, even when a speaker is supporting a diplomatic initiative. Similarly, positive language about international cooperation does not necessarily indicate approval of a particular foreign policy.
Dictionary methods have difficulty interpreting context, negation, sarcasm, and the subject toward which an opinion is directed.


d. Positions and polarity —
could you place speakers on a scale from their words? Against what would you validate it?
Senate Foreign Relations Committee hearings
Speakers could potentially be positioned along a defined policy dimension using their statements. However, different hearings may address unrelated foreign policy questions, making a single ideological scale difficult to interpret.
Wordfish could estimate relative positions from word frequencies, but the resulting dimension would require substantive validation. I would first identify a specific policy issue and restrict the analysis to relevant statements.
The estimated positions could then be compared with independently coded statements, recorded votes where relevant, or documented positions on the issue.

1. YouTube Comments
Producer and audience: YouTube users produce comments for other viewers, video creators, and participants in online discussions. Comments may express opinions about data center development, electricity costs, environmental concerns, and local economic impacts.
Unit and quantity: The primary unit is an individual comment. We will collect comments from videos identified using data-center-related search terms. The final number of comments will depend on the number of relevant videos, API availability, and collection limits. We have currently captured 800,000 comments for review over thousands of videos.
Collection and permission: We will use the YouTube Data API v3 with an authorized API key. Requests will follow Google’s API policies and quota restrictions.
Known gap: YouTube commenters are self-selected and cannot be assumed to represent U.S. public opinion. Comments may also be removed, moderated, or unavailable through the API.


2. Congressional Candidate Websites
Producer and audience: U.S. House and Senate candidates and their campaign organizations produce official websites to communicate policy positions to voters, supporters, journalists, and potential donors.
Unit and quantity: The primary unit is a webpage or policy statement discussing data centers. We intend to examine the websites of candidates competing in the 2026 congressional elections. The number of relevant documents will depend on how many candidates address the issue. We have already examined tens of thousands of pages over 1,100+ websites.
Collection and permission: Campaign websites will be examined for references to data centers and related terms. Relevant pages may be collected through respectful web scraping or manual collection, subject to each website’s terms and applicable access restrictions.
Known gap: Campaign websites represent curated political communications rather than complete records of candidate opinions. A candidate who does not mention data centers cannot automatically be classified as neutral or opposed.


3. News Articles
Producer and audience: Journalists, editors, and news organizations produce articles for general audiences, local communities, policymakers, and subscribers. Coverage may describe proposed data centers, public opposition, environmental concerns, and political responses.
Unit and quantity: The primary unit is a news article. We plan to collect relevant articles published during the 2026 election cycle. The final count will depend on search terms, source coverage, and access to article text. We expect to view several thousand news articles over November 30, 2025 through November 3, 2026.
Collection and permission: Media Cloud is a potential discovery source for identifying relevant news coverage. Full-text collection would require access through permitted APIs, publisher websites, or other authorized sources. Article metadata and full text must be distinguished.
Known gap: News coverage reflects editorial decisions and newsworthiness rather than the prevalence of public attitudes. Local controversies may receive extensive coverage, while less visible developments may receive little attention.

The World Bank values are 2024 annual observations, while Wikipedia reports country-specific values with different reporting dates. Therefore, many of the differences may reflect different reporting vintages rather than directly comparable measurements from the same period. Large discrepancies may also reflect differences in measurement or reporting conventions and should be investigated individually before being interpreted as changes in reserves.
This comparison includes only countries whose names match in both datasets because the tables were combined using an inner_join(). Countries missing from either source or recorded under different country names are excluded from the comparison.


c.
In two sentences: when is scraping the right tool?
Scraping is the right tool when the data are publicly available on a webpage but there is no structured way to access it. When an API or structured dataset is available, use that because it is reproducible, and less dependent on changes to the webpage’s HTML structure.
Wikipedia is a poor scraping target. It is volunteer-edited, has no schema, no versioning and no stated uncertainty, and the table shape changes without notice so the parser breaks silently. It also has a documented API and bulk dumps, which means scraping it is a choice one did not have to make. Scrape when there is no other way in.

title: Assignment 4
text:
4. Data plan
Write one page: a plan to acquire web data for your own research.

a.
The primary source will be Media Cloud, using its online news archive to identify news articles related to data centers. Media Cloud is appropriate because it is designed specifically for media research and provides a large, searchable collection of online news sources. We will constrain our searches of this database by keywords and dates. This will create the URLs that we will scrape for our corpus. The list of publisher URLS will then be queried for text data. Media Cloud itself does not make its extracted article text available for download because of copyright restrictions.


b.
What robots.txt and the Terms of Service permit
Media Cloud will be used to identify article URLs rather than as the target of scraping. Its Terms of Service permit lawful academic, nonprofit, and journalistic research but prohibit unreasonable use of bandwidth or exceeding API limits. Because the article text will be collected from individual publishers, each publisher’s robots.txt rules and Terms of Service would be applied for scraping them. Pages that prohibit automated access will not be collected. Media Cloud does not grant permission to reproduce third-party article content.


c.
Whether an API exists — and your justification if you scrape anyway
Media Cloud provides a search API, but we will generate a CSV so that we can preprocess the URL dataset.
Scraping is still necessary for the next stage because Media Cloud does not provide downloadable full article text. Where permitted, the URLs returned by the API will therefore be used to retrieve the original publisher pages and extract their article text.


d.
Volume, rate limiting, and how you will cache
Collection will be incremental rather than downloading the entire corpus at once. Our collection program will be respectful and implement delays and retries rather than repeatedly issuing requests after errors.
Successfully collected records will be cached locally and written to Parquet. Each record will contain the article text together with identifying and provenance fields such as source, source ID, URL, title, author when available, publication date, collection date, language, search query, and collection method. Before requesting an article again, the program will check whether it has already been successfully collected. This allows the program to be rerun without repeatedly downloading the same material.


e.
What breaks when the page changes, and how you will notice?
Scraping article text from publishers is always error prone because HTML structure differs among publishers and will change over time. A selector that identifies article text today may stop finding it after a site redesign, or it may begin capturing navigation, advertising, or other material instead.
The collection process will retain collection-status information and validate scraped results before treating them as successful. Missing text, unusually short text, HTTP errors, unexpected content, or changes in expected fields will be recorded as collection failures rather than cached as valid articles. Primary collection is via rvest, but on a failure, we also have implemented an Rselenium backup process. Because successful articles are already stored in the Parquet database, a change to a publisher’s website should require recollecting only failed or new records rather than rebuilding the entire corpus.Initial pipeline testing will be limited, with the collection volume expanded after the scraping and storage workflow has been validated.

The public (Part 1). Tweets collected during the summit: frequent words, hashtag and mention networks, LSA. This dataset is archived — the API that produced it no longer offers that access, so it cannot be collected again.

The archive contains tweets posted around the November 2021 meeting. I used the text of each tweet as one document. Retweets and repeated posts are still in the file, so the results describe the collected tweets, not a group of unique people.

The frequent words show what appeared most often in this archive. They do not show what the public as a whole believed. The search terms, collection period, repeated posts, and the people who chose to use Twitter all shaped the results.

The mention network is more fragmented and contains separate news, political, and entertainment groups. This is another sign that the archive contains several conversations rather than one unified response to the summit.
LSA groups tweets by similarities in their word use. Each point is one tweet. The axes do not come with a ready-made political meaning, so I would need to read the words and tweets that define each side before naming the patterns.

The government (Part 2). Collect every document in the Compilation of Presidential Documents (GovInfo, CPD) mentioning “Xi Jinping” since 20 January 2021. Read Xi in context with kwic(), then use keyness to compare the Biden and Trump administrations.

The code searches the CPD collection for the exact phrase "Xi Jinping" in documents published since January 20, 2021. It goes through every page of results and downloads the text supplied by GovInfo. If the key is missing, it stops instead of showing made-up results.

govinfo_key <- Sys.getenv("GOVINFO_API_KEY")
cpd_available <- nzchar(govinfo_key)

govinfo_search_all <- function(query, api_key, page_size = 1000) {
  offset <- "*"
  pages <- list()

  repeat {
    response <- request("https://api.govinfo.gov/search") |>
      req_url_query(api_key = api_key) |>
      req_body_json(list(
        query = query,
        pageSize = as.character(page_size),
        offsetMark = offset,
        resultLevel = "package",
        sorts = list(list(field = "publishdate", sortOrder = "ASC"))
      )) |>
      req_perform()

    payload <- resp_body_json(response, simplifyVector = FALSE)
    pages <- append(pages, list(payload$results))

    new_offset <- payload$offsetMark
    if (length(payload$results) == 0 || is.null(new_offset) || identical(new_offset, offset)) break
    offset <- new_offset
  }

  purrr::list_flatten(pages)
}

scalar_chr <- function(x) if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) NA_character_ else as.character(x[[1]])

if (cpd_available) {
  cpd_query <- 'collection:(CPD) AND "Xi Jinping" AND publishdate:range(2021-01-20,)'
  cpd_retrieved_at <- format(Sys.time(), tz = "UTC", usetz = TRUE)
  cpd_results <- govinfo_search_all(cpd_query, govinfo_key)

  cpd_index <- tibble(
    package_id = map_chr(cpd_results, ~ scalar_chr(.x$packageId)),
    title = map_chr(cpd_results, ~ scalar_chr(.x$title)),
    date_issued = as.Date(map_chr(cpd_results, ~ scalar_chr(.x$dateIssued))),
    text_link = map_chr(cpd_results, ~ {
      link <- .x$download$txtLink
      if (is.null(link)) link <- .x$download$htmlLink
      scalar_chr(link)
    })
  ) |>
    distinct(package_id, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
    filter(!is.na(text_link))

  read_govinfo_text <- function(url) {
    response <- request(url) |>
      req_url_query(api_key = govinfo_key) |>
      req_perform()

    page <- response |>
      resp_body_string() |>
      read_html()

    # Keep the document body, but stop before GovInfo's appended index fields.
    blocks <- page |>
      html_element("body") |>
      xml2::xml_children()

    block_text <- blocks |>
      html_text2() |>
      str_squish()

    metadata_start <- which(str_detect(block_text, "^Categories:"))[1]
    if (!is.na(metadata_start)) {
      block_text <- block_text[seq_len(metadata_start - 1)]
    }

    block_text |>
      discard(~ .x == "") |>
      paste(collapse = "\n")
  }

  cpd_docs <- cpd_index |>
    mutate(text = map_chr(text_link, read_govinfo_text)) |>
    # The GovInfo search can match an index field even when the name is not
    # used in the document itself. Retain only body text that names Xi Jinping.
    filter(str_detect(text, regex("\\bXi\\s+Jinping\\b", ignore_case = TRUE)))

  cpd_index <- cpd_index |>
    semi_join(cpd_docs, by = "package_id")

  cpd_corpus <- corpus(cpd_docs, text_field = "text", docid_field = "package_id")
  docvars(cpd_corpus, "title") <- cpd_docs$title
  docvars(cpd_corpus, "date_issued") <- cpd_docs$date_issued

  # Reproducibility files contain metadata only—not document text or the API key.
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

  cpd_manifest <- cpd_index |>
    mutate(
      query = cpd_query,
      retrieved_at_utc = cpd_retrieved_at
    )

  cpd_log <- tibble(
    endpoint = "https://api.govinfo.gov/search",
    query = cpd_query,
    result_level = "package",
    sort = "publishdate ASC",
    retrieved_at_utc = cpd_retrieved_at,
    packages_with_text = nrow(cpd_manifest)
  )

  write_csv(cpd_manifest, "data/cpd_manifest.csv")
  write_csv(cpd_log, "data/cpd_collection_log.csv")

  tibble(
    documents = ndoc(cpd_corpus),
    first_publication = min(cpd_docs$date_issued, na.rm = TRUE),
    last_publication = max(cpd_docs$date_issued, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
} else {
  cat("CPD collection not run: set GOVINFO_API_KEY and render again.\n")
}

For the comparison, documents published before January 20, 2025 are labeled Biden and later documents are labeled Trump. Keyness finds words used more often by one administration than the other. It does not tell us by itself whether either president approved of a policy or how important the topic was.

After the appended index fields are removed, the Biden documents are more closely associated with words such as press, briefing, security, national, and adviser. The Trump documents are more closely associated with words such as tariffs, reporters, people, great, and president. These differences may partly reflect the kinds of documents published under each administration, so they should not be treated as a direct measure of policy positions.

Compare: what does each source let you say about the summit, and about US–China relations? Who produced each text, and for whom?

The tweets show immediate public discussion by Twitter users, journalists, organizations, and possibly automated accounts. They help identify common words, hashtags, and mentioned accounts in the collected stream. They cannot tell us what Americans as a whole thought because Twitter users chose whether to post, and repeated or popular posts can give a few voices more weight.
The CPD documents are official remarks and statements prepared by presidents and their staffs for the public, reporters, other officials, and foreign governments. The Office of the Federal Register edits and publishes them. They show how each administration spoke publicly about Xi and US–China relations, but not what was said privately or how the public reacted. The query also leaves out documents that used a different name for Xi. The two sources therefore answer different questions: the tweets show part of the public conversation, while the CPD documents show the government’s public message.

Wordfish assumes that word counts follow a Poisson process. It allows for some speeches being longer, some words being common everywhere, and some words being especially useful for separating speeches along one line. In this case, the results appear to capture a mix of time period and presidential language, with recent speeches generally apart from several early postwar speeches. 3. Collect it from R

a. gtrends package
Use the gtrendsR package and the gtrendsR01.R program. The first call in that script is the same query you just ran by hand:

library(gtrendsR)
library(readr)

# Store successful Google Trends downloads here.
cache_dir <- "_gtrends_cache"
dir.create(cache_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Download each query only once. If Google temporarily blocks the request,
# retry with exponential backoff until a successful result is returned.
# Once saved as an RDS file, future renders read the local file and never
# contact Google Trends for that query again.
cached_gtrends <- function(cache_name, ..., initial_wait = 60, max_wait = 600) {
  cache_file <- file.path(cache_dir, cache_name)

  if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
    return(readRDS(cache_file))
  }

  attempt <- 1L

  repeat {
    result <- tryCatch(
      gtrends(...),
      error = function(e) {
        message(
          "Google Trends request failed on attempt ", attempt,
          ": ", conditionMessage(e)
        )
        NULL
      }
    )

    if (!is.null(result)) {
      saveRDS(result, cache_file)
      message("Google Trends data saved to: ", cache_file)
      return(result)
    }

    wait <- min(initial_wait * 2^(attempt - 1L), max_wait)
    wait <- wait + runif(1, 0, 15)
    message("Retrying in ", round(wait), " seconds...")
    Sys.sleep(wait)
    attempt <- attempt + 1L
  }
}

b. What are the differences between the two methods? Consider at least:

i. Reproducibility — could someone else regenerate your file exactly?
Neither method guarantees that another person can reproduce the exact values by making a new request, because Google Trends draws from sampled data and a moving “last five years” window. The R method makes the procedure more reproducible because the code records the query and analysis steps. Exact numerical reproduction depends on retaining and sharing the cached raw data used for the analysis.


ii. Provenance — which method records the query parameters for you?
The R method provides stronger provenance because the function call explicitly records the search terms, geography, time window, category, and search type. The website download requires those selections and the pull time to be documented manually in a datasheet; the CSV alone does not preserve the complete collection procedure.


iii. Scale — what happens when you need fifty terms instead of three?
Collecting fifty terms manually would require many repeated website searches and downloads, increasing both labor and the risk of inconsistent settings. R can automate the repeated calls, file naming, validation, and caching. However, the terms must still be divided into batches because the service limits comparisons, and the batches need a shared anchor term if their separately normalized indices are to be placed on a common scale.


iv. Fragility — what breaks, and how would you know?
The website method is vulnerable to interface changes, inconsistent manual selections, and misplaced downloads. The R method depends on gtrendsR and an unofficial endpoint, so changes to the service can break requests or parsing; rate limiting can also return errors such as HTTP 429. Failures should be detected by checking request errors, expected columns, date ranges, row counts, missing values, and the 0–100 range before analysis. Caching the first successful pull prevents later endpoint failures from changing an already completed analysis.

text:
4. Prepare answers — analytics of text data

How are text data generated? Who wrote the text, for whom, and what decided which texts you can collect?

In general text is generated by people writing, although that will be changing in the future. The content reflects an author’s purpose, intended audience, and the context for which it was produced.
What texts can be collected are determined by social, legal and mechanical constraints. Social is defined by our morals and ethics. Legal is defined by our laws. Mechanical is defined by what is actually available.

What is a topic, and what would convince you a topic model found one?

A topic is a common theme or subject found across documents. Topic models identify groups of words that often appear together, helping researchers find themes in large collections of text.
To decide whether a model found meaningful topics, I would look at the words associated with each topic and read some of the documents individually. The topics should make sense, be different from one another, and appear consistently when the model is run again. I would also compare the results with human analysis.
For our data center research, topics might include electricity use, water consumption, economic development, and local opposition. A good model would identify these themes and connect them to documents that actually discuss those issues.

What does a sentiment score measure — and what does a dictionary miss?

A sentiment score measures how positive or negative a text is. Dictionary-based methods assign values to words and combine them to estimate the overall tone of a document. Some methods also measure emotions such as fear, anger, etc.
Dictionary methods have limitations because they often miss context, sarcasm, and how words are used. For example, the word “power” might be positive in one context but neutral when discussing electricity.
For our data center research, sentiment scores could help show differences in how data centers are discussed. However, a positive or negative score does not necessarily mean the author supports or opposes data centers. It could just be based on quotes. Comparing the scores with documents reviewed by people would help determine how accurate the results are.

How would you place a text on a position or polarity scale, and against what would you validate it?

A text can be placed on a scale using dictionaries, classification models, or statistical methods such as Wordfish. These methods estimate where a document falls between two positions, such as supporting or opposing a policy.
For our data center research, I would use a scale ranging from opposition to support. A model could be trained using documents that people have already classified, with neutral or mixed positions placed near the middle.
To check the results, I would compare the model’s scores with documents independently reviewed by people. I would also check whether different reviewers agree and whether the model produces consistent results across sources. This is important because a document might discuss negative environmental effects while still supporting data center development.

3. Research

a. Survey
Survey the R packages for web scraping. At minimum look at rvest, httr2, polite, RSelenium and chromote.


b. Compare
Choose two to compare. For each, be ready to say: what does it assume the page looks like, what does it do about JavaScript, and what does it do about rate limiting?








Question
rvest
RSelenium




What does it assume the page looks like?
Assumes the desired content is available in the returned HTML, where it can be selected using CSS selectors or XPath.
Treats the site as a browser-rendered page and interacts with it much like a user would.


What does it do about JavaScript?
Does not execute JavaScript. Content generated only after JavaScript runs generally will not be available to rvest alone.
Uses a real browser/WebDriver, so JavaScript executes. It can scrape dynamically generated content and interact with buttons, forms, scrolling, etc.


What does it do about rate limiting?
Nothing automatically. You need to control request frequency yourself, for example with delays or by combining it with polite.
Nothing specifically for rate limiting. Browser interaction is naturally slower than simple HTTP requests, but request frequency still needs to be deliberately controlled.





c. robots.txt
What is robots.txt? Who writes it, who reads it, and what happens if you ignore it?
robots.txt is a small text file that a website can place at the root of its domain. It tells automated programs, especially web crawlers and scrapers, which parts of the site the site owner would prefer them to access or avoid. The site administrator writes it, but can be autogenerated. Crawlers, bots, etc. read it. It is not an access control mechanism, so it can be ignored easily.
If you ignore it, several things can happen:

The site may detect your scraper and throttle or block your IP address.
You may get 403, 429 Too Many Requests, CAPTCHAs, or other anti-bot responses.
Your behavior may violate the site’s Terms of Service.
You may impose an unwanted load on the website.
In some circumstances, there could be legal issues.



d. Find two
Find two websites’ robots.txt and analyse them. Append /robots.txt to any domain. For each file, identify:

i. the User-agent blocks — does the site treat all crawlers alike?


ii. what is Disallowed, and what is explicitly Allowed


iii. any Crawl-delay and any Sitemap


iv. whether the scrape you have in mind would be permitted
Check it from R, not by eye. The robotstxt package reads the file for you: robotstxt::paths_allowed("https://example.com/some/page"). The polite package wraps that check together with rate limiting, so compliance is the default rather than an afterthought.
